title: Time with nuance
goal: Go beyond sudah and belum: say what you managed or didn't manage to do (sempat), what has only just happened (baru), what is under way (tengah), what you have ever done (pernah), and how often (jarang, kadang-kadang), in both formal and everyday Indonesian.
bekal: explain what happened and what didn't with *telah, sempat, belum sempat*
use *baru* for "just", "only so far" and "not until"
tell *pernah* from *sudah* and talk about frequency: *jarang, kadang-kadang*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Laporan yang terlambat
dialogs.intro: The last week of March 2028. The monthly report to UGM is overdue, and Dr. Lestari has come to the project office in Sumberwangi to ask why. Yoga is there too, looking guilty.

lines.text: Mohon maaf, Bu. Laporannya tengah kami selesaikan. Minggu ini agak kacau.

lines.text: Baik. Kadang-kadang lapangan memang lebih penting daripada laporan. Tapi hanya kadang-kadang.

notes: **Kendala** means "obstacle, snag, hitch", and *Ada kendala?* is the tactful way for a superior to ask "what went wrong?". It lets you explain without admitting fault. In reports you will see *kendala teknis* (technical problems) and *kendala di lapangan* (difficulties in the field).

**Bukan? at the end** turns a statement into "isn't it?" in careful speech: *Survei sudah selesai, bukan?* In everyday talk the same job is done by *kan* or *ya*: *Udah selesai, kan?* Dr. Lestari, being precise and academic, uses the full form.

**Yoga says saya.** In Unit 2 Yoga used *aku* with Sarah. Here, with his own lecturer, he switches to *saya* and drops his slang. Indonesians change pronouns according to who is listening, sometimes several times in one conversation, and nobody finds it odd.

**Kena air** — "got hit by water". *Kena* is the everyday way of saying something happened to you: *kena hujan* (caught in the rain), *kena macet* (stuck in traffic), *kena tilang* (got a traffic ticket). It sits close to the ke-…-an adversative you know from A2.

**Kapan-kapan** is "some time, one of these days", without a date. *Kapan-kapan main ke rumah, ya* (come round some time) is sincere but not a firm invitation; it is the Indonesian "we must do lunch". Dr. Lestari, however, will probably hold Sarah to it.

**Begadang** means to stay up late or all night, usually by choice or necessity rather than insomnia. Students *begadang* before exams, neighbours *begadang* on a *ronda* (night watch). A famous dangdut song warns: *Begadang jangan begadang, kalau tiada artinya*.

grammars.title: The formal and the fine-grained markers
body: You already have *sudah, belum, sedang, akan, masih*. Add these and you can report on a project the way a professional does, in speech or in writing.
after: *Sempat* is the word English speakers never find on their own, and it is everywhere. It means there was an opportunity or a window of time, and the action fitted into it. *Belum sempat* is the gentlest possible way to say you haven't done something: not refused, not forgotten, just not yet found the time.
⚠️ *Telah* and *sudah* mean the same, but *telah* in a chat with a friend sounds like a newsreader. Use it in reports, speeches and formal emails.

grammars.title: pernah vs sudah
body: *Sudah* says an action is complete; *pernah* says it is part of your experience, at least once, at some point. English uses "have done" for both, which is why learners mix them.

head: Indonesian
English
What it means
rows: at some past time, now over

after: Dr. Lestari says *belum pernah*, not *tidak pernah*: "I haven't been, yet", leaving the door open. *Tidak pernah* would sound as if she had no intention of going.
⚠️ *Pernah* is not a general past tense. For something on a specific date, use a time word: *Kemarin saya ke sana*, not ✗ *Kemarin saya pernah ke sana*.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Minggu yang sibuk
dialogs.intro: Saturday evening in Yogyakarta. Sarah is back in her rented house for the weekend, and Bu Endang and her grandson Dimas, now eleven, come to the gate as soon as they see her motorbike.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Lho, Mbak Sarah! Baru pulang to? Sekarang kok jarang kelihatan.
lines.id: Well, Mbak Sarah! You've only just got back? We hardly ever see you these days.
lines.literal: [lho], Miss Sarah! just go-home [to]? now [kok] rarely visible.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Iya, Bu, baru sampai tadi sore. Sekarang saya jarang di Yogya, paling cuma Sabtu-Minggu.
lines.id: Yes, I only got in this afternoon. I'm hardly ever in Yogya now, just at weekends at most.
lines.literal: yes, Madam, just arrive earlier afternoon. now I rarely in Yogya, most only Saturday-Sunday.

lines.id: Yes, I have, Dimas. Yesterday there was a little snake at the edge of a rice field.
lines.literal: ever, Dim. yesterday there-is snake small at edge rice-field.

lines.id: Ooh, how scary. So what's kept you busy this week?

lines.text: Tapi Mbak sempat-sempatnya upload foto pakai kebaya!

lines.text: Oh iya, Dimas sudah tunjukkan ke Eyang. Ayu tenan, Mbak!

lines.text: Ya sudah, istirahat dulu. Pasti belum sempat masak, to? Nanti saya antar sayur lodeh.
lines.id: Well, have a rest. I bet you haven't had time to cook, have you? I'll bring you some vegetable stew.
lines.literal: yes already, rest first. surely not-yet get-chance cook, [to]? later I deliver vegetable lodeh.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Belum sempat, Bu. Matur nuwun, lho.
lines.id: No, I haven't. Thank you so much.

notes: **Baru pulang to?** — "only just back, then?" *Baru* + verb is "have just", and in Javanese-flavoured Indonesian *to* at the end asks for agreement, like *kan*. Bu Endang's *lho* at the start shows pleased surprise. You met both in A2; here they arrive in one breath.

**Kok jarang kelihatan** — "how come you're so rarely seen?" The *kok* marks mild surprise, not criticism. Telling someone they have been hard to find is a warm way of saying "we've missed you". The polite answer explains, as Sarah does, rather than apologising.

**Pernah lihat ular belum?** Dimas asks with *pernah … belum?*, the natural spoken way to ask "have you ever …?": *Pernah ke Bali belum?* The answer is *pernah* (yes, I have) or *belum* (not yet). Children and adults alike use this pattern constantly.

**Sempat-sempatnya** — "fancy (you) finding the time to…". Doubling *sempat* and adding *-nya* adds a teasing, slightly incredulous tone: with all that work, you still managed to post a photo! It can be affectionate, as here, or a genuine rebuke: *Sempat-sempatnya main HP waktu rapat!*

**Eyang, tenan.** Bu Endang calls herself *Eyang* (grandma, Dimas's word for her) because she is talking in front of her grandson; families often speak from the child's point of view. *Tenan* is Javanese for "really, truly"; *ayu tenan* is "really lovely". In Indonesian: *cantik sekali*.

**Matur nuwun** is Javanese for "thank you", politer than the Indonesian-flavoured *makasih*. Sarah has picked it up from her neighbours, and using it with an older Javanese woman is a small, much-appreciated courtesy. The reply is *sami-sami* (you're welcome).

grammars.title: How often? From always to never
body: Frequency words sit before the verb, like the aspect markers. Here is the scale, with the everyday forms you will actually hear.
after: *Jarang* is a full word in its own right; you do not need *tidak* with it. *Saya jarang di Yogya* is "I'm rarely in Yogya". ⚠️ ✗ *Saya tidak jarang* means "I'm not rarely", which is to say quite often.
*Sering* also means "frequently" in the sense of "a lot, many times": *Saya sering ke Magelang* (I go to Magelang a lot). *Sering-sering main ke sini, ya!* is "do come round more often!"

blocks.text: *Baru* began life as "new", and it still means that. But before a verb, a time or a number it does three other jobs, all of them about something being early, recent or incomplete.

head: Meaning
Example
English
rows: He has only just gone home.
Only half the data is in so far.
The report won't be ready until Friday.

blocks.text: The "not until" meaning is the one to watch. *Dia baru datang jam sepuluh* is not "he has just come at ten" but "he didn't come until ten", and a little complaint is usually hiding in it.
The root *sempat* is about having an opening in time. Its family is small and extremely useful for being polite about what you did not do.

blocks.title: Sempat as a past marker
items: In speech and news, *sempat* can simply mean "did, at one point, for a while": *Harga cabai sempat naik* (chilli prices went up for a while).
It often implies the situation later changed: *Saya sempat ragu, tapi akhirnya setuju* (I had my doubts for a while, but in the end I agreed).
*Maaf, belum sempat membalas* is the standard opening of a late reply to a message. Learn it; you will need it.
